bava_kamma-11a-10-11.note: A man borrowed an ax from another man and broke it. He came before Rav, who told him: go and pay him with a good, whole ax. Rav Kahana and Rav Asi asked Rav, Is this the law? and Rav was silent.
bava_kamma-11a-10-11.why: The Gemara is unsure whether, by Shmuel's account, a court values a broken item for a borrower, so the owner takes it back and the borrower pays only the loss. Rav's order first seems to say no; his silence before his students is read as yes, and the law follows them.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who ordered the borrower to replace the ax.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Questioned Rav's ruling, with Rav Asi.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: Questioned Rav's ruling, with Rav Kahana.

terms.meaning: When a court appraises a damaged item, the owner keeps the item at its reduced value and the one responsible pays only the difference.

bava_kamma-19b-16-16.note: A donkey ate some bread and broke the basket it was kept in. Rav Yehuda ruled that its owner must pay the full damage for the bread but only half the damage for the basket.
bava_kamma-19b-16-16.why: The Gemara is sorting animal damage into normal eating, which costs full damages, and unusual acts, which cost half. Asked why the basket is not part of eating, it answers that the donkey ate first and only then broke the basket.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who ruled on the donkey's damage.

terms.meaning: An owner pays the whole loss when his animal does harm in its normal way, such as eating; for an unusual act, like goring, by an animal not known for it, he pays half.

bava_kamma-20a-0-0.note: A goat saw a turnip on top of a clay barrel. It climbed up, ate the turnip, and broke the barrel. Rava made its owner pay full damages for both the turnip and the barrel.
bava_kamma-20a-0-0.why: The Gemara has just explained why a donkey that broke a basket after eating cost only half. Here it explains Rava's full award: since a goat normally eats turnips, climbing to reach one is normal too, so the broken barrel counts as part of eating.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled the goat's owner fully liable.

terms.meaning: Payment of the whole loss, owed when an animal does harm in its normal way, as when eating.

bava_kamma-20b-1-1.note: Rami bar Hama told Rav Hisda that the question he had raised was already answered in a mishna. Rav Hisda asked which mishna, and Rami bar Hama said he would tell him after Rav Hisda served him. Rav Hisda took Rami bar Hama's scarf and folded it, and Rami bar Hama then quoted it: if the animal benefits, its owner pays for the benefit it derived.
bava_kamma-20b-1-1.why: The question is whether a squatter in a courtyard that would never have been rented must pay for the benefit he got, though the owner lost nothing. Rami bar Hama offers the mishna as the answer, and Rava then remarks that the two cases are not really alike.

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: The Sage who said a mishna answered the question, once he had been served.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The Sage who asked, and folded Rami bar Hama's scarf as a service.

terms.meaning: The earliest written collection of Jewish law, on which the Gemara comments.

bava_kamma-21a-8-8.note: A man built a mansion on a garbage heap that belonged to orphans. Before that, nomadic Carmanians had lived on the site and paid the orphans a small sum. Rav Nahman told the man to go and appease the orphans, but he paid no attention, so Rav Nahman confiscated his mansion.
bava_kamma-21a-8-8.why: The Gemara has cited Rav's view that one who lives in another's courtyard without permission need not pay rent. It asks whether Rav Nahman's ruling disagrees, and answers no: here the orphans lost real income from the Carmanians.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The Sage who told the builder to appease the orphans and then confiscated his mansion.

terms.meaning: Nomadic tribespeople who had lived on the orphans' land and paid them a little for it.

bava_kamma-27b-11-12.note: Two people shared a cistern and took turns drawing water from it, one each day. One of them came to draw on a day that was not his. The other said, This is my day, but he paid no attention, so the other took the handle of a hoe and struck him. Rav Hisda sent the case to Rav Nahman, who answered that he should have struck him a hundred times with the hoe.
bava_kamma-27b-11-12.why: Rav Hisda had asked what fine applies to a blow with a hoe, and Rav Nahman wanted the facts first. His answer leads into the dispute over taking justice into one's own hands, which, Rav Nahman says, everyone allows when a loss would otherwise follow.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The Sage who sent the case of the cistern to Rav Nahman.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The Sage who said the striker was right to strike.

terms.term: Take justice into one's own hands
terms.meaning: To enforce one's own rights directly, without going to a court first.

bava_kamma-36b-11-16.note: A man slapped another. Rav Toviya bar Mattana asked Rav Yosef whether the sela fine set for a slap means the valuable Tyrian sela or the small provincial one. They argued it from a mishna about a gold dinar, and it was settled by Rav's rule, quoted by Rav Yehuda: coins in the Torah are Tyrian, coins in the Sages' rulings are provincial, so the fine is half a dinar. The man who was slapped said that for so little he did not want it; let it go to the poor. Then he changed his mind and asked for it to live on. Rav Yosef told him the poor had already acquired it, since the court acts as the hand of the poor.
bava_kamma-36b-11-16.why: The Gemara has turned to a mishna that sets a sela as the fine for a slap, against Rabbi Yehuda's hundred dinars; this case fixes what that sela is worth. Rav Yosef's last ruling leads into the rule that a court likewise acts for orphans.

people.name: Rav Toviya bar Mattana
people.about: A Sage who sent the slapping case to Rav Yosef and argued with his answer.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who answered, and ruled the fine belonged to the poor.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Quoted Rav's rule on Torah and rabbinic coinage.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage whose rule on coinage settled the question.

terms.meaning: A silver coin. A Tyrian sela was worth four dinars; a provincial sela only half a dinar.
A Sage of the mishna's era; here, the author of the mishna.
The court acts as the legal agent of the poor, so it can take possession for them.

bava_kamma-37a-2-2.note: Hanan the wicked slapped a man, and the case came before Rav Huna, who told him to go and pay the man half a dinar. Hanan had a clipped dinar and wanted to pay half of it, but no one would take it to give him change. So he slapped the man again and gave him the whole clipped dinar.
bava_kamma-37a-2-2.why: The Gemara has just fixed the fine for a slap at a provincial sela, half a dinar. This second slapping case shows that sum ordered in practice.

people.name: Hanan the wicked
people.about: A man who slapped another, then slapped him again.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage who fined Hanan half a dinar.

terms.meaning: A coin with its edge trimmed, which people were unwilling to accept or change.

bava_kamma-38a-12-12.note: The Roman government once sent two military officials to the Sages of Israel with an order: teach us your Torah. They read it through three times. As they left, they said they had examined the whole Torah and found it true, except for one rule: if a Jew's ox gores a gentile's ox the owner is exempt, but if a gentile's ox gores a Jew's ox he pays in full. Either the Torah's words of another apply only to Jews, and then the gentile should be exempt too, or they apply to everyone, and then the Jew should pay too. But they said they would not report this to the government.
bava_kamma-38a-12-12.why: The Sages tell this story in connection with the rule the officials challenge, the different treatment of a Jew's ox and a gentile's ox, which the Gemara has just been discussing.

terms.meaning: An innocuous ox has no record of goring and its owner pays half the damage; a forewarned ox has gored before and its owner pays in full.
Words from the Torah's law of goring oxen, about an ox that gores the ox of another person.

bava_kamma-38a-14-15.note: The daughter of Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda died. The Sages asked Ulla to come with them to console him, but he refused: the Babylonians console mourners by saying what can be done, which implies they would act against God's decree if they could, and he called that heresy. He went alone and spoke to the father about God telling Moses not to make war on Moab. Moses had reasoned that if the Torah ordered Israel to strike the Midianites, who only helped Moab, then surely Moab itself should be attacked. God answered that He had two good fledglings to bring out of them, Ruth the Moabite and Naamah the Ammonite. Ulla reasoned that if God spared two great nations for two such women, then if the daughter had been righteous and fit to bring good into the world, she would surely have lived.
bava_kamma-38a-14-15.why: The story is told in passing after the account of the Roman officials, and its mention of Moab and Ammon leads the Gemara on to a teaching that God rewards even refined speech.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
people.about: A Sage whose daughter died; Ulla calls him his teacher.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: He refuses the Babylonian form of consolation and goes alone to comfort the father.

people.name: Moses
people.about: In Ulla's words, he reasoned that Moab should be attacked and God stopped him.

people.name: Ruth the Moabite
people.about: Named by God as one of the two good fledglings for whose sake Moab was spared.

people.name: Naamah the Ammonite
people.about: Named by God as the other good fledgling, for whose sake Ammon was spared.

terms.meaning: An argument from a lesser case to a greater one: if this is true here, it is all the more true there.
Neighboring peoples who, in the Torah, joined against Israel in the wilderness.

bava_kamma-41b-6-7.note: Shimon HaAmasoni, or by another account Nehemya HaAmasoni, drew a lesson from every occurrence of the word et in the Torah. When he reached You shall fear et the Lord your God, he stopped. His students asked what would become of all the interpretations he had already made. He said: just as I received reward for expounding, I receive reward for withdrawing. Later Rabbi Akiva came and taught that et in that verse includes Torah scholars.
bava_kamma-41b-6-7.why: The Gemara has explained that one tanna derives the ban on a stoned ox's hide from the word et, while another does not read et for new rules at all. This baraita shows that method of reading and the point where it was abandoned.

people.name: Shimon HaAmasoni
people.about: A Sage who interpreted every et in the Torah until he reached the fear of God.

people.name: Nehemya HaAmasoni
people.about: The name some give the same Sage.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Later taught that the et in the verse includes Torah scholars.

terms.meaning: A small Hebrew word that marks the object of a verb and is not translated. Some Sages read each occurrence as adding something to the verse.

bava_kamma-48a-5-5.note: A woman went into a house to bake. The homeowner's goat came and ate her dough, became overheated and died. Rava made the woman pay for the goat.
bava_kamma-48a-5-5.why: The Gemara is asking who is liable when one person's animal or goods are on another's property. It asks whether Rava's ruling clashes with Rav, who exempts produce brought in without permission, and answers that she came in with permission and so took on responsibility.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who made the woman pay for the goat.

bava_kamma-50a-18-20.note: Neḥunya, a digger of pits, ditches and caves, used to dig wells and hand them over to the public, and the Sages said he had kept this rule too. Once his daughter fell into a large cistern, and people told Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa. After the first hour he said she was at peace, after the second the same, and after the third he said she had come up. Asked who brought her up, she said a ram had come to her, led by an old man. They asked Rabbi Ḥanina whether he was a prophet; quoting Amos, he said he was not, but had reasoned that the offspring of that righteous man should not stumble through the very thing he had toiled over.
bava_kamma-50a-18-20.why: The Gemara is discussing liability for pits near the public road; a teaching that a digger who hands a well over to the public is exempt names Neḥunya as the example, and Rabbi Aḥa then adds that even so his son died of thirst.

people.name: Neḥunya
people.about: A digger of pits, ditches and caves who made wells for public use; the father of the girl who fell into the cistern.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa
people.about: The Sage who was told of the girl's fall and announced, hour by hour, that she was safe and then that she had come up.

terms.meaning: A rule of Jewish law. The Sages say Neḥunya kept this one too, handing his wells over to the public.

bava_kamma-50b-1-2.note: A man was throwing stones from his own property into the public road. A pious man found him and said: Lowlife, why are you throwing stones from property that is not yours into property that is yours? The man mocked him. Some days later he had to sell his field, and while walking along that same public road he stumbled on those same stones. He said: That pious man put it well.
bava_kamma-50b-1-2.why: The story comes with the Sages' rule that a person should not clear stones from his land into the public road, part of the wider discussion of hazards people leave in public places, which the next mishna continues with pits dug there.

terms.meaning: Land open to everyone, such as a street or road, as opposed to a person's private property.

bava_kamma-50b-16-17.note: An ox fell into a water channel, and its owner slaughtered it. Rav Naḥman declared it a tereifa, an injured animal that may not be eaten. He added that if the owner had spent a kav of flour and gone to learn in the study hall, he would have known that an animal that lives a full day after such a fall is fit to eat, and he would not have lost an ox worth several kav.
bava_kamma-50b-16-17.why: The Gemara is debating whether a fall into a pit less than ten handbreadths deep can do deadly harm by impact. From this case it infers that Rav Naḥman held it can, and Rava then challenges him from the mishna.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The Sage who ruled the slaughtered ox forbidden and said the owner lost it through not knowing the law.

terms.meaning: A measure of volume. Rav Naḥman's point is that a small cost in flour would have saved an ox worth far more.
The place where the Sages and their students studied and taught the law.

bava_kamma-51a-0-0.note: Continuing his argument with Rava over the ox that fell into a water channel, Rav Naḥman says that a pit less than ten handbreadths deep is exempt when an animal dies in it because its fumes are not strong enough to kill. Rava asks how the digger can then be liable when an animal is only injured there. Rav Naḥman answers that the fumes are not enough to kill but are enough to injure.
bava_kamma-51a-0-0.why: The Gemara is testing whether Rav Naḥman's ruling on the ox fits the mishna, which exempts a shallow pit if an animal dies in it. Rava goes on to challenge him from the height of the platform used for stoning.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The Sage defending his ruling about the ox that fell into a water channel.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who challenges Rav Naḥman's ruling from the mishna.

terms.meaning: The Gemara's word for the bad air at the bottom of a pit, thought able to kill or harm an animal that falls in.
A measure about the width of a hand. The mishna treats ten handbreadths as the depth of a pit that can kill.

bava_kamma-58b-14-15.note: A man cut down another man's date palm. They came before the Exilarch, who said he had seen the place himself: three palms stood there in one cluster, worth a hundred dinars together, so the man must pay thirty-three and a third. The man said: Why should I be judged by the Exilarch, who rules by Persian law? He went to Rav Naḥman, who ruled that the damage is valued against an area sixty times larger. Rava asked Rav Naḥman whether that rule, said of damage done by a person's property, also holds for damage a person does with his own body.
bava_kamma-58b-14-15.why: The Gemara has just explained that damage to a field is valued against an area sixty times larger. Here Rav Naḥman applies that to a felled tree, and Rava's question opens the debate that follows on damage done directly by a person.

people.name: the Exilarch
people.about: The judge who first heard the case and valued the palm as a third of the cluster.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The Sage the man turned to, who valued the damage against an area sixty times larger.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who questioned whether Rav Naḥman's rule applies to damage done by a person himself.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, who also acted as a judge.
A silver coin.

bava_kamma-59a-19-19.note: Eliezer Ze'eira was standing in the market of Neharde'a wearing black shoes. Officials of the Exilarch's house asked why, and he said he was mourning Jerusalem. Thinking it presumptuous, they put him in prison. He said he was a great scholar and offered to prove it, and they told him to ask. He asked what someone who cuts the flower cluster of another's date palm must pay, and knocked down each answer they gave. Asked for his own answer, he said the damage is valued against an area sixty times larger, and told them Shmuel and his court could confirm it. They sent to Shmuel, who said he was right, and they released him.
bava_kamma-59a-19-19.why: The Gemara has been weighing how to value a damaged date palm, setting the sixty-times rule against the Exilarch's approach. In this story Shmuel himself confirms the sixty-times rule.

people.name: Eliezer Ze'eira
people.about: A scholar jailed for wearing black shoes in mourning for Jerusalem, who won his release by a legal question.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage whose court was asked, and who confirmed Eliezer Ze'eira's ruling.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia; here his officials have the power to arrest and release.

bava_kamma-74b-18-19.note: Rabban Gamliel blinded the eye of his slave Tavi and was overjoyed, because a slave whose master blinds his eye goes free. He met Rabbi Yehoshua and asked: Do you know that my slave Tavi has gone free? Rabbi Yehoshua asked why, and Rabban Gamliel said: Because I blinded his eye. Rabbi Yehoshua told him his words meant nothing, since there were no witnesses.
bava_kamma-74b-18-19.why: Rav Huna, citing Rav, holds that a man who admits to an act carrying a fine stays exempt even if witnesses come later. Rav Ḥisda cites this case against him: it implies that with witnesses Rabban Gamliel would have had to free Tavi despite admitting it first.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Tavi's master, who blinded his slave's eye and was glad of it.

people.name: Tavi
people.about: Rabban Gamliel's Canaanite slave.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: The Sage who told Rabban Gamliel that without witnesses his admission did not free Tavi.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Reports Rav's ruling that admitting to a fine exempts a person even if witnesses come later.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Raises this incident as an objection to Rav Huna.

terms.meaning: A payment the Torah sets as a penalty rather than as repayment of an actual loss. Freeing a slave whose eye was blinded is treated as one, and a fine is not imposed on a person's own admission.
A non-Jewish slave held by a Jewish master.

bava_kamma-80a-3-5.note: A pious man was suffering from pain in his heart. The physicians said his only remedy was to suckle warm milk every morning, so a she-goat was brought and tied to the leg of his bed. Days later his friends came to visit, saw the goat, and turned back, saying: There is an armed bandit in this man's house, and we are going in to him? They looked into his conduct and found no sin but the goat, and at his death he himself said it was his only sin, because he had gone against the words of his colleagues.
bava_kamma-80a-3-5.why: Rabban Gamliel has just allowed keeping such an animal for a while only if it is tied to the legs of the bed and does not graze with the flock. The pious man did just that, yet the story still counts it as his one sin.

bava_kamma-80a-9-9.note: A woman's son was causing her grief, and she jumped up and swore: Any man who comes to marry me, I will not turn away. Unworthy men jumped at the chance. When the matter came before the Sages, they said she had meant only a man suited to her.
bava_kamma-80a-9-9.why: The teaching just before says a man who vowed to buy a house or marry a woman in the Land of Israel need not take the first one he finds but may wait for one suited to him. This incident reads a woman's oath the same way.

bava_kamma-80a-12-13.note: Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, said that in Babylonia they had taken on themselves the Land of Israel's ban on raising sheep and goats. Rav Adda bar Ahava asked Rav Huna about his own animals. Rav Huna said his wife Ḥova watched over them. Rav Adda bar Ahava said: May Ḥova bury her son! For all the years of Rav Adda bar Ahava's life, no children of Rav Huna by Ḥova survived. Another version says the ban took hold in Babylonia only from the time Rav came there.
bava_kamma-80a-12-13.why: The baraita under discussion bans raising small domesticated animals in the Land of Israel. This exchange asks whether the ban also binds Jews in Babylonia, and how strictly.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage cited as saying Babylonia took on the Land of Israel's ban.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Reports Rav's statement about the ban in Babylonia.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: Challenges Rav Huna over his animals and curses his wife's children.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Keeps sheep and goats, saying his wife Ḥova guards them.

people.name: Ḥova
people.about: Rav Huna's wife, who watched over his animals.

terms.meaning: Sheep and goats. The Sages banned raising them in the Land of Israel.
The Land of Israel.

bava_kamma-80a-14-14.note: Rav, Shmuel and Rav Asi came to a celebration for a newborn son (some say for the redemption of a firstborn). None would go in ahead of another: Rav not before Shmuel, Shmuel not before Rav Asi, Rav Asi not before Rav. They decided Shmuel would wait while Rav and Rav Asi went in. The Gemara explains that Rav deferred to Shmuel only as a gesture, because of an incident in which he had cursed him. Meanwhile a cat came and severed the baby's hand. Rav went out and taught that a cat may be killed, may not be kept, and is protected neither by the laws of theft nor by the duty to return lost property.
bava_kamma-80a-14-14.why: The baraita being discussed lists animals one may or may not raise, and one view allows cats because they clear houses of vermin. Rav's ruling after this incident forbids keeping one, and the Gemara goes on to reconcile the two.

people.name: Rav
people.about: One of the three Sages at the celebration; after the cat attack he ruled against keeping cats.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: One of the three Sages, who stayed behind so the others could enter.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: The third Sage; he would not go in before Rav.

terms.meaning: A celebration for a newborn boy; the translation takes it as a circumcision.
A ceremony in which a father redeems his firstborn son from a priest with a payment.

bava_kamma-81b-9-10.note: Rabbi and Rabbi Ḥiyya were walking on a road and stepped off to its sides. Ahead of them, Rabbi Yehuda ben Kanosa was taking long strides along the road itself. Rabbi asked who this was, showing off his greatness before them. Rabbi Ḥiyya said it might be his student Rabbi Yehuda ben Kanosa, all of whose actions were for the sake of Heaven. When they reached him and Rabbi saw him, he said: If you were not Yehuda ben Kanosa, I would have cut off your legs with iron shears.
bava_kamma-81b-9-10.why: The Gemara is going through Joshua's conditions for the land, one of which lets travelers step off a rough road onto private land. Here great Sages use that right, and Rabbi treats passing it up as a show of pride.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, walking with Rabbi Ḥiyya; he took the man ahead for a show-off.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Rabbi's companion, who said the man was probably his own student.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Kanosa
people.about: Rabbi Ḥiyya's student, who kept to the road instead of stepping off it.

terms.meaning: Done out of real devotion to God rather than for one's own glory.

bava_kamma-82b-15-17.note: When the Hasmonean royal house was at war with itself, Hyrcanus was inside Jerusalem and Aristobulus outside. Each day those inside lowered coins in a box, and those outside sent up animals for the daily offerings. An elder there who knew Greek wisdom told the besiegers that as long as the Temple service went on, the city would not be handed over to them. The next day, when the coins came down, they sent up a pig. When it reached the middle of the wall it dug its hooves in, and the Land of Israel quaked over four hundred parasangs by four hundred. At that time the Sages said: Cursed is the man who raises pigs, and cursed is the man who teaches his son Greek wisdom. A mishna records that in that time the barley and wheat for two Temple offerings had to come from distant places.
bava_kamma-82b-15-17.why: The mishna rules that no one may raise pigs anywhere, and this account is given as the background to that rule. The Gemara then asks whether Greek wisdom is really forbidden.

people.name: Hyrcanus
people.about: The Hasmonean who was inside besieged Jerusalem.

people.name: Aristobulus
people.about: The Hasmonean besieging Jerusalem from outside.

terms.meaning: The Jewish royal family that ruled the Land of Israel; here two of its members are at war.
The sacrifices brought in the Temple every morning and afternoon.
Greek learning; the Sages cursed whoever taught it to his son.
A Persian measure of distance, a few miles long.

bava_kamma-83a-0-2.note: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel applied the verse "My eye affected my soul, because of all the daughters of my city" to his own family: there were a thousand children in his father's household, five hundred studying Torah and five hundred studying Greek wisdom, and the only ones left were himself and his cousin in Asia Minor. The Sages explained that Rabban Gamliel's household was different because it was close to the government, just as they allowed Avtolmos bar Reuven, who was also close to the government, to cut his hair in the Roman style.
bava_kamma-83a-0-2.why: The Gemara has cited a curse on anyone who teaches his son Greek wisdom; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's account seems to show it was studied freely in his father's house, and the Sages explain why that family was an exception.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: He tells of the thousand children in his father's household, of whom only he and a cousin remained.

people.name: Avtolmos bar Reuven
people.about: A man close to the government who was allowed to wear the Roman-style haircut.

terms.meaning: Greek learning and culture, which the Sages restricted at a time of war with Rome.
A Roman hairstyle; adopting it was treated as following the ways of the gentiles.
Gentile customs that the Torah forbids Jews to imitate.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core text the Gemara discusses.

bava_kamma-83a-7-7.note: A woman went into a house to bake, and a dog barked at her. Its owner told her not to be afraid, since its canine teeth had been removed. She answered: Take your favors and throw them on the thorns! The baby has already moved.
bava_kamma-83a-7-7.why: Rabbi Dostai has just taught that a dog that frightens a pregnant woman into miscarrying can drive the Divine Presence from Israel. This incident shows a dog doing that harm even without its teeth, within the discussion of restrictions on raising dogs.

bava_kamma-84a-20-21.note: A donkey severed a child's hand, and the case came before Rav Pappa bar Shmuel. He told the court officers to assess four types of payment. Rava objected that the mishna lists five; Rav Pappa bar Shmuel said he meant besides the damage itself. Abaye objected that a donkey's owner pays only for damage, so he told them to assess the damage. Asked whether the child had to be valued as a slave, he said yes. The child's father refused, saying it would demean the boy. Told he was acting against the child, he said that when the boy grew up he would appease him with his own money.
bava_kamma-84a-20-21.why: The Gemara has just discussed how an injured person's loss is measured, including whether the court values him as if he were a slave. This case puts that method into practice, and a similar case before Rava follows.

people.name: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel
people.about: The judge in the case of the child's severed hand.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Objects that the mishna lists five types of payment, not four.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Objects that a donkey's owner pays only for the damage itself.

terms.meaning: The mishna's list of what someone who injures a person must pay: the damage, pain, medical costs, lost time and humiliation.
Measuring an injury by how much it would lower a person's price if he were sold as a slave.

bava_kamma-88a-20-20.note: The mother of Rav Shmuel bar Abba of Hagroneya, who was married to Rabbi Abba, signed her property over to her son. After she died, Rav Shmuel bar Abba went to Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba, who confirmed him as owner. Her husband, Rabbi Abba, took the matter to Rav Hoshaya, who brought it to Rav Yehuda; Rav Yehuda cited Shmuel that a husband can take back property his wife sold in his lifetime. Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba answered from a mishna about a father who signs property over to his son, and Rav Yehuda replied, again citing Shmuel, that this case is not like that mishna. The text does not say who finally kept the property.
bava_kamma-88a-20-20.why: The case becomes a test of whether owning the right to a property's produce counts as owning the property itself, the point Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish dispute. Afterward Rav Yosef and Abaye argue over why Shmuel set the two cases apart.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Abba
people.about: The son to whom his mother signed over her property.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: His mother's husband, who contested the gift.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
people.about: The judge who confirmed the son as owner and defended his ruling from a mishna.

people.name: Rav Hoshaya
people.about: Brought Rabbi Abba's complaint to Rav Yehuda.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Cited Shmuel's rulings against the son's claim.

terms.meaning: Property a wife owns while her husband has the right to its produce and income.
The early collection of Jewish law on which the Gemara comments.

bava_kamma-91a-20-22.note: In the mishna's incident, a man uncovered a woman's head in the marketplace, and Rabbi Akiva made him pay her for the humiliation. Given time to pay, the man waited until she stood at the door of her courtyard and got her to uncover her own head. The Gemara asks how he could be given time, when Rabbi Ḥanina says no time is given for injuries, and answers that humiliation, unlike injury, causes no money loss. It then cites a baraita in which Rabbi Akiva told the man: You dived into mighty waters and came up with a potsherd in your hand, for a person may injure himself.
bava_kamma-91a-20-22.why: The Gemara has been asking whether humiliation payments are scaled to the victim's standing; Rabbi Akiva holds that even the poor deserve full payment. His case is then tested against other rulings on time to pay and on harming oneself.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage who made the man pay for humiliating the woman.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: Says the court gives no time to pay for injuries.

terms.meaning: One of the payments owed for harming someone: compensation for the shame caused.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

bava_kamma-91b-15-15.note: A man slaughtered an animal or bird, and someone else got there first and covered its blood. Rabban Gamliel ruled that the second man must pay the slaughterer ten gold coins.
bava_kamma-91b-15-15.why: Rav has just explained a claim for payment of the form 'I wanted to do this commandment myself.' A baraita teaches that the one who slaughters must cover the blood, and this case is the precedent for paying a man who was robbed of that commandment.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who made the man who covered the blood pay the slaughterer.

terms.meaning: The Torah's command that whoever slaughters a wild animal or bird must cover its blood with dust.

bava_kamma-92a-1-1.note: Shmuel's sharecropper brought him dates, and Shmuel tasted wine in them. He asked why, and the sharecropper said the palms stood among the grapevines. Shmuel said: Do they weaken the vines that much? Tomorrow bring me from their marrow, meaning cut the palms down.
bava_kamma-92a-1-1.why: The Gemara has just taught when a fruit tree may be cut down despite the ban on destroying trees. Shmuel's order to fell palms that drew strength from more valuable vines is a case in point, and Rav Ḥisda does the same just after.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The landowner who tasted wine in his dates and had the palms cut down.

terms.meaning: A farmer who works another's land in return for a share of the crop.
The soft heart of a palm, which can be taken only by cutting the tree down.

bava_kamma-93a-17-18.note: A purse of charity money arrived in the city of Pumbedita, and Rav Yosef deposited it with a certain man. The man was careless with it, and thieves came and stole it. Rav Yosef held him liable to pay. Abaye challenged him with a teaching that the bailee's duty covers money given to safeguard, not money given to distribute to the poor. Rav Yosef answered that the poor of Pumbedita each had a fixed sum set aside for them, so this money counted as money to safeguard, and the man had to pay.
bava_kamma-93a-17-18.why: The Gemara has just been asking when a bailee is responsible for an item that came into his possession for safeguarding rather than for some other purpose; this case tests that line with charity funds.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who deposited the charity purse with the man and ruled him liable when it was stolen.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Challenges Rav Yosef's ruling with a teaching about money meant for the poor.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law; the Gemara often quotes one to challenge or support a ruling.
Someone entrusted with another person's property to look after; Jewish law sets out when he must pay if it is lost or stolen.

bava_kamma-94b-5-5.note: Rabbi Yohanan says a certain ruling dates from the days of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and cites a teaching to show it. A man who wanted to repent of his thieving was told by his wife: "Empty one! If you repent, even the belt you are wearing is not yours." He held back and did not repent. At that time the Sages declared that when robbers or lenders who took interest return what they took, it should not be accepted from them, and the Sages are displeased with anyone who does accept it.
bava_kamma-94b-5-5.why: The Gemara has just quoted this ruling as part of its discussion of the ordinance made to ease the way for those who repent; Rabbi Yohanan's story explains where the ruling came from. The Gemara then tests it against a teaching about children who inherit money taken as interest.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage who dates the ruling and cites the story as its origin.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply "Rabbi"; the ruling was taught in his days.

terms.meaning: Lenders who charge interest; Torah law forbids Jews to take interest from one another, so such money must in principle be returned.
To turn back from wrongdoing; for a thief, true repentance includes returning what he stole.

bava_kamma-96b-6-8.note: A man robbed another of a pair of oxen, plowed and sowed his field with them, and eventually returned them. The owner came before Rav Nahman, who ordered that the increase in the land's value be estimated and paid. Rava objected that the land had improved partly on its own; Rav Nahman said he meant only half the increase. Rava pressed that a stolen item is simply returned as it was. Rav Nahman replied: Did I not tell you not to say anything to me while I sit in judgment? Our friend Huna said I am the equal of King Shapur in monetary law. This man is an old robber, and I want to penalize him.
bava_kamma-96b-6-8.why: The Gemara is explaining the mishna's principle that all robbers pay according to the value at the time of the robbery. Rava quotes that very rule, and Rav Nahman's reply shows a judge going beyond it to fine a habitual robber.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who orders the robber to pay part of the land's increase in value, as a penalty.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Questions Rav Nahman's ruling while he is sitting in judgment.

people.name: Huna
people.about: Called "our friend" by Rav Nahman, who quotes him praising Rav Nahman's authority in monetary law.

terms.meaning: Here a nickname: the translation explains it as Shmuel, a leading authority on monetary law, so Rav Nahman is claiming equal standing with him.
A ruling from the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law on which the Gemara comments.

bava_kamma-97a-4-6.note: Rav Yosef bar Hama's household would seize the slaves of people who owed him money and put them to work. His son Rabba asked why. Rav Yosef bar Hama cited Rav Nahman: a slave is not worth even the bread in his stomach. Rabba answered that Rav Nahman meant a slave like his own Daru, who only danced among the wine barrels; other slaves do real work. His father then cited Rav's ruling that one who seizes another's slave and works him owes nothing. Rabba replied that this holds only when no money is owed; for a creditor it looks like interest. Rav Yosef bar Hama said: I retract.
bava_kamma-97a-4-6.why: The Gemara has just argued that an owner is glad to have his slave kept working, so one who uses another's slave need not pay. The story shows the limit: when the user is the owner's creditor, the same use looks like interest.

people.name: Rav Yosef bar Hama
people.about: A creditor whose household put his debtors' slaves to work; he retracts when his son objects.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Son of Rav Yosef bar Hama, who questions his father's practice.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Sage quoted on both sides of the argument; Daru was his slave.

people.name: Daru
people.about: Rav Nahman's slave, who, Rabba says, only danced among the wine barrels.

people.name: Rav Daniel bar Rav Ketina
people.about: Sage who reports Rav's ruling that one who works another's slave is exempt.

terms.meaning: Payment for the use of a loan. Torah law forbids Jews to take it from one another, and the Sages also forbade anything that merely looks like it, such as a creditor getting free labor from a debtor.

bava_kamma-99b-23-23.note: A woman showed a dinar coin to Rabbi Hiyya, who told her it was good. The next day she came back and said others had told her it was bad, and she could not spend it. Rabbi Hiyya told Rav to go and exchange it for her, and to write in his notebook: this was a bad transaction.
bava_kamma-99b-23-23.why: The Gemara has ruled that an expert money changer who misjudges a coin is exempt. It then asks why Rabbi Hiyya, himself an expert, paid, and answers that he acted beyond the letter of the law.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: The Sage who judged the woman's coin to be good and then replaced it.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sent by Rabbi Hiyya to exchange the coin and record the mistake.

terms.meaning: A silver coin in common use at the time.

bava_kamma-103a-3-3.note: Rav Kahana paid in advance for flax and left it with the seller. The price of flax rose, and the seller sold it. Rav Kahana came to Rav and asked whether he should go and take his money. Rav told him: if, when they sold it, they said "This flax is Kahana's," go and take it; if not, do not take it.
bava_kamma-103a-3-3.why: The Gemara has been discussing purchases made on someone else's behalf. It then asks whose view Rav's ruling follows, and concludes that the worry was that taking the higher price would look like interest on money paid in advance.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Paid in advance for flax, which the seller later sold after its price rose.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage Rav Kahana consulted about whether he could take the money.

terms.meaning: A plant grown for its fibers, which are spun into linen.

bava_kamma-103b-9-9.note: Rava tells of a pious man who bought something from one of two people and did not know which one. He came to Rabbi Tarfon, who told him to place the price between them and walk away. He then came to Rabbi Akiva, who told him he had no remedy until he paid each of them in full. Rava argues that a pious man would never have sworn a false oath.
bava_kamma-103b-9-9.why: The Gemara had suggested that Rabbi Akiva demands payment to every possible owner only from someone who swore falsely. Rava uses this pious buyer to challenge that limit, since Akiva made the same demand of him.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage who tells the incident to challenge an explanation of Rabbi Akiva's view.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: Tells the buyer to leave the price between the two sellers and walk away.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Tells the buyer he must pay each of the two sellers.

terms.meaning: A person known for strict and careful observance. The Gemara says that when it speaks of "a certain pious man" it means one of two Sages who were pious all their lives.
Swearing in court that something untrue is true, for example that one owes nothing. It is a serious sin and brings extra penalties.

bava_kamma-104b-1-2.note: Rabbi Abba was owed money by Rav Yosef bar Hama, and asked Rav Safra to bring it back with him. When Rav Safra arrived, Rava, Rav Yosef bar Hama's son, asked whether Rabbi Abba had given him a written receipt. He had not, so Rava told him to go and get one first. Then Rava changed his mind: even a receipt was worthless, since Rabbi Abba might die before Rav Safra returned, and the money would belong to his orphans. Rav Safra asked what could be done. Rava told him to have Rabbi Abba transfer the debt to him along with a piece of land, then come and write the receipt himself.
bava_kamma-104b-1-2.why: Shmuel has ruled that a debtor may not send payment through someone carrying the creditor's sign. The Gemara asks what a creditor can do under that rule, and this case gives the answer.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Creditor who asks Rav Safra to collect his debt from Rav Yosef bar Hama.

people.name: Rav Yosef bar Hama
people.about: Owes money to Rabbi Abba; his son Rava handles the payment.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: Sent by Rabbi Abba to bring back the money.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Son of Rav Yosef bar Hama, who explains what Rav Safra needs before his father can pay him.

terms.meaning: The wording of a receipt in which a creditor confirms the debt was paid, protecting the debtor from being asked to pay again.
A legal device: rights that cannot be handed over on their own, such as a debt, are transferred together with a piece of land, which can be.

bava_kamma-104b-3-3.note: Rav Pappa was owed twelve thousand dinars by someone in Bei Hozai. He transferred his claim to Rav Shmuel bar Abba, together with the threshold of his house. When Rav Shmuel bar Abba came back with the money, Rav Pappa went out as far as Tavakh to meet him.
bava_kamma-104b-3-3.why: The Gemara has just explained that a creditor can collect through a messenger by transferring the debt to him together with land. Rav Pappa's case shows that method being used.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A creditor owed twelve thousand dinars, who transfers the debt to Rav Shmuel bar Abba to collect it.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Abba
people.about: Receives the claim and brings back the money.

terms.meaning: A silver coin in common use at the time.
A small piece of real estate. Handing it over lets the debt be transferred along with it, since land can carry other property with it in a transfer.

bava_kamma-112a-13-14.note: Rabbi Yirmeya's brother-in-law, a minor, shut the doors of his late father's house against Rabbi Yirmeya, who claimed part of it. Rabbi Yirmeya took the case to Rabbi Avin, who said the boy was holding what was his. Rabbi Yirmeya offered witnesses that he had taken possession while the father was alive, but Rabbi Avin said testimony is not accepted in the absence of the other party, and a minor cannot stand as one. Rabbi Yirmeya protested: had the whole world lined up behind Sumakhos to take away what was his? The case reached Rabbi Abbahu, who cited a ruling that land a child seizes is taken from him at once, and he may bring witnesses when he grows up. The Gemara rejects that comparison, since this boy inherited the house; the text does not say how the case ended.
bava_kamma-112a-13-14.why: The Gemara has just cited a teaching on whether minor heirs must return what their father stole, with Sumakhos disagreeing; this case turns on that dispute and leads into a discussion of testimony given when a party is absent.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: He claims a share of his father-in-law's house and is shut out by his young brother-in-law.

people.name: Rabbi Avin
people.about: The judge who first hears the case and favors the boy.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: The Sage the case finally reaches; he cites a ruling in Rabbi Yirmeya's favor.

people.name: Sumakhos
people.about: An early Sage who held that minor heirs are exempt; Rabbi Avin points to his view.

terms.meaning: A child under the age of legal adulthood, who cannot be a party to a court case.
A legal assumption that whoever holds property, here by inheriting it, owns it unless proven otherwise.

bava_kamma-113a-5-6.note: Rav Asi visited Rav Kahana's house. He saw that Rav Kahana had summoned a certain woman to court in the evening, and by morning, when she had not come, had written a document banning her. Rav Asi asked whether he did not hold with Rav Hisda that a court sets dates on Monday, Thursday and Monday first. Rav Kahana replied that this is for a man, who may be away from town for reasons beyond his control. A woman is always in town, so if she does not come, she is rebellious.
bava_kamma-113a-5-6.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rav Hisda's rule of three court dates before a ban is written; this case tests that rule against Rav Kahana's quicker practice with a woman.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: Visits Rav Kahana and questions his quick ban on a woman.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Judge who banned a woman the morning after she failed to appear.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: Sage whose rule of three court dates Rav Asi cites.

terms.meaning: A court order placing someone under a ban, cutting them off from normal dealings with the community until they comply.
Here, someone who defies the court on purpose, as opposed to someone kept away by circumstances.

bava_kamma-113b-11-11.note: Rav Ashi was traveling on the road and saw clusters of grapes hanging on a vine in an orchard. He told his attendant to go and see whose they were: if they belonged to a gentile, bring some; if to a Jew, bring none. A gentile sitting in the orchard heard him and asked: Is it permitted to take from a gentile? Rav Ashi answered that a gentile takes money for his grapes, while a Jew does not.
bava_kamma-113b-11-11.why: The Gemara has been discussing what a Jew owes a gentile: returning lost items, and benefiting from a gentile's business mistakes. This is the last in a series of incidents on that theme.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Traveling Sage who wants to take grapes only if he can pay for them.

people.name: the gentile
people.about: Sitting in the orchard; he overhears Rav Ashi and challenges him.

terms.meaning: A person who is not Jewish.
A student or servant who travels with a Sage and runs errands for him.

bava_kamma-114b-19-20.note: Shmuel told of a man who said, just in passing, that he remembered being a small child riding on his father's shoulder. They took him from school, took off his tunic and immersed him so he could eat teruma, the priests' portion of produce, that evening. In Rabbi Hanina's telling he added: my friends kept away from me and called me "Yohanan, eater of hallot." On the strength of what he said, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi raised him to the priesthood.
bava_kamma-114b-19-20.why: Rav Ashi has said that remarks made in passing are relied on only for letting a woman remarry and in matters of rabbinic law. The Gemara cites this case against him, since eating teruma is a matter of Torah law.

people.name: Yohanan
people.about: The man whose memories of eating teruma as a child led to his acceptance as a priest.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply "Rabbi"; he raised Yohanan to the priesthood on the strength of his words.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage who tells the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: Sage who adds the ending about the friends' nickname.

terms.meaning: Mentioning a fact in passing, without trying to prove anything. Such remarks are sometimes trusted even from people who could not testify formally in court.
Dipped in a ritual bath to become ritually pure, which a priest must be before eating teruma.
The portion of dough given to priests. Like teruma, only priests may eat it.
The status of being a kohen, a descendant of Aaron, with rights such as eating teruma.

bava_kamma-115a-13-13.note: Rav Huna was a student of Rav. A thief known as Hanan the Wicked stole a cloak and sold it. When the case came before Rav Huna, he told the man whose cloak was stolen: Go redeem your pledge, meaning pay back the buyer and take the cloak.
bava_kamma-115a-13-13.why: Rav has said that the Sages did not apply the marketplace rule here, so a buyer can recover his money only from the thief. The Gemara cites this ruling by Rav's own student against that, then answers that Hanan, who had no money, was a special case.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A student of Rav who judged the case of the stolen cloak.

people.name: Hanan the Wicked
people.about: A thief who stole a cloak and sold it.

terms.term: provision ensuring the integrity of the marketplace
terms.meaning: An ordinance of the Sages: when a stolen item is found with someone who bought it in good faith, the owner must repay the buyer's price to get it back, so that ordinary buying and selling stays safe.

bava_kamma-115a-21-22.note: Avimi bar Nazi, Ravina's father-in-law, was owed four dinars by a man. The man stole a cloak and brought it to him, and Avimi then lent him four more dinars. In the end the man was found to be the thief, and the case came before Ravina. He ruled that for the first four dinars the owner owes Avimi nothing, but for the four later dinars Avimi should take his money from the owner and return the cloak.
bava_kamma-115a-21-22.why: The Gemara has just ruled that the marketplace ordinance protects buyers of stolen goods, but not a creditor repaid with stolen goods. Ravina applies that line to a case with both kinds of loan; Rav Kohen objects and Rabbi Abbahu rules with him.

people.name: Avimi bar Nazi
people.about: Ravina's father-in-law, who lent money to a man who brought him a stolen cloak.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: The judge who splits the case between the two loans.

terms.meaning: A silver coin in common use at the time.

terms.term: ordinance ensuring the integrity of the marketplace
terms.meaning: A rule of the Sages that an owner must repay a good-faith buyer before taking back a stolen item, so that ordinary trade stays safe.

bava_kamma-115a-24-25.note: A man from Naresh stole a scroll and sold it to a man from Pappunya for eighty dinars, who sold it on to a man from Mehoza for one hundred and twenty. Then the thief was identified. Abaye ruled that the owner should pay the man from Mehoza eighty dinars and take back his scroll, and the man from Mehoza should collect the other forty from the man from Pappunya. Rava objected and ruled instead that the owner pays the full one hundred and twenty, then collects forty from the man from Pappunya and eighty from the thief from Naresh.
bava_kamma-115a-24-25.why: The Gemara is working through cases of the Sages' ordinance that an owner pays to reclaim stolen goods from an innocent buyer; this case asks how it applies when the item passes through a second buyer.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: He gives the first ruling on how the payments should be divided.

people.name: Rava
people.about: He objects to Abaye and gives a different division.

terms.meaning: An ordinance of the Sages: an owner who reclaims stolen goods from an innocent buyer repays the buyer's price, so that people are not afraid to buy in the market.
A silver coin.

bava_kamma-116a-9-9.note: Rav Safra was traveling with a caravan, and a lion followed along with them. Every night the travelers sent the lion one of their donkeys, and it ate it. When Rav Safra's turn came, he sent his donkey, but the lion did not eat it. Rav Safra hurried and took it back as his own.
bava_kamma-116a-9-9.why: Rav has just ruled that someone who sets out to rescue another's donkey on the promise of payment is still paid if his own donkey comes out of the river by itself: mercy came to him from Heaven. Rav Safra's donkey is compared to that case.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: A traveler in a caravan whose donkey the lion did not eat.

terms.meaning: A group of travelers journeying together for safety, with their pack animals.
Took formal ownership. Having given the donkey up to the lion, Rav Safra treated it as ownerless and took possession of it again.

bava_kamma-116b-20-21.note: A man showed thugs where the Exilarch's household kept its piles of wheat, and they seized them. Rav Nahman ruled that the man must pay. Rav Huna bar Hiyya, seated before him, with Rav Yosef behind, asked whether this was the law or a fine. Rav Nahman said it was the law, from the mishna about one who showed a field to thugs. After he left, Rav Yosef asked Rav Huna bar Hiyya why it mattered. He answered: if it is the law, we learn from it for other cases; if it is a fine, we do not.
bava_kamma-116b-20-21.why: The mishna has just ruled that one whose actions caused thugs to seize a field must replace it, and the Gemara explained this as a case of showing them the field. This case applies that reading and asks whether such rulings set precedent.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who orders the man to pay for the wheat.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Hiyya
people.about: Seated before Rav Nahman; asks whether the ruling was law or a fine.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Seated behind Rav Huna bar Hiyya; later asks him why the question mattered.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, a powerful official with his own household and estates.
A penalty a court imposes to deter wrongdoing, beyond what the strict law requires; a fine in one case does not set a rule for others.
A ruling from the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law on which the Gemara comments.

bava_kamma-117a-12-13.note: Gentiles forced a man to show them the wine of Rav Mari, son of Rav Pinehas, son of Rav Hisda. Then they told him to carry it and bring it along with them, and he did. The case came before Rav Ashi, who exempted him from paying. The Rabbis objected that a teaching makes one who hands property over with his own hands liable. Rav Ashi answered that this applies only when he did not lead them to the property at the start. Once he had, it was as if the wine were already burned.
bava_kamma-117a-12-13.why: The Gemara has just cited a teaching that one forced to show property to gentiles is exempt, but one who hands it over himself is liable. This case falls between the two, and Rav Ashi draws the line.

people.name: Rav Mari
people.about: Son of Rav Pinehas, son of Rav Hisda; the owner of the wine the gentiles took.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The judge who exempts the man from paying for the wine.

terms.meaning: People who are not Jewish; here, men who coerce a Jew into helping them seize property.
Here, the scholars present with Rav Ashi, who question his ruling.

bava_kamma-117a-17-24.note: A man insisted, twice, that he would show another man's straw to the gentile authorities, though Rav forbade it; Rav Kahana, sitting before Rav, broke his neck and killed him. Warning that the new Greek rulers punish bloodshed, Rav sent Kahana to the Land of Israel to study under Rabbi Yoḥanan, on condition he raise no objections for seven years. Kept silent, Kahana was moved back to the last row, then stood up and out-argued Rabbi Yoḥanan, who removed his seven cushions one by one. Seeing Kahana's split lips, Rabbi Yoḥanan thought he was smirking; he was offended and Kahana died. Told it was only his look, Rabbi Yoḥanan got past a serpent at the burial cave by calling himself the disciple, prayed, and raised Kahana, who answered all his questions.
bava_kamma-117a-17-24.why: The Gemara is discussing who must pay when someone hands another's property to gentile officials; this story shows how gravely the Sages treated a man who would inform on a fellow Jew's property, and a run of informer cases follows.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The teacher who forbade the man to inform, then sent Rav Kahana away to the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Rav's student, who killed the would-be informer and later out-argued Rabbi Yoḥanan.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Also called Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish; he reviewed Rabbi Yoḥanan's lecture and called Rav Kahana a lion.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Head of the academy in the Land of Israel; an old man whose offense caused Rav Kahana's death, and who revived him.

terms.meaning: The Land of Israel.
A legal ruling or teaching of Jewish law.
Rabbi Yoḥanan sat raised on cushions so all the students could see him; removing them one by one lowered himself before Rav Kahana.

bava_kamma-117b-3-6.note: Someone showed Rabbi Abba's silk to gentiles, who seized it. Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappi and Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa sat to judge whether the informer must pay, with Rabbi Ile'a beside them. They thought to hold him liable, from a mishna that a judge who rules wrongly pays from his own pocket, but Rabbi Ile'a quoted Rav that this applies only when the judge took and handed over the money himself. They sent Rabbi Abba to Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim and Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat, who held the informer liable.
bava_kamma-117b-3-6.why: The Gemara is collecting cases of people who pointed out a fellow Jew's property to gentiles; this one asks whether causing a loss by words alone, without taking the property, brings an obligation to pay.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: The owner of the silk that was seized.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: One of the three judges who first heard the case.

people.name: Rabbi Ile’a
people.about: Sat beside the judges and quoted Rav to limit the mishna they relied on.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim
people.about: One of two judges who rule on indirect damage, and who held the informer liable.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat
people.about: The other judge who rules on indirect damage, and held the informer liable.

terms.meaning: The early collection of rabbinic law on which the Gemara is a commentary; also a single teaching from it.
Loss a person causes without doing the harm with his own hands; some judges held people liable for it and some did not.

bava_kamma-117b-8-8.note: A man was holding a purse of money collected to ransom captives. Thieves came upon him, and he took the purse and gave it to them. Rabba exempted him from paying it back. Abaye objected that the man had saved himself with someone else's money; Rabba answered that there is no greater redemption of captives than this.
bava_kamma-117b-8-8.why: It is one of a series of cases before Rabba about people who give up another's property to save themselves; just before, a man who handed thieves a deposited silver cup was judged by whether he was rich.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: The judge who exempted the man.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Objected that the man saved himself with another's property.

terms.meaning: Paying ransom to free Jews held captive, counted among the most important uses of charity money.

bava_kamma-117b-9-9.note: A man hurried his donkey onto a ferry before the other passengers boarded. The donkey was about to sink the boat, so another man pushed it into the river and it drowned. Rabba exempted him from paying. Abaye objected that he had saved himself with another's property; Rabba answered that the donkey's owner had been a pursuer from the start.
bava_kamma-117b-9-9.why: The Gemara notes this fits Rabba's general rule: a pursuer's property may be destroyed to save his victim, but a person may not save himself with a bystander's property.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: The judge who exempted the man who drowned the donkey.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Objected that the man saved himself with another's property.

terms.meaning: In Jewish law, someone who puts another person's life in danger; he may be stopped by any means needed, including destroying his property.

bava_kamma-119a-7-7.note: Rav Ḥisda had a sharecropper who would weigh out the produce and give Rav Ḥisda his share, and weigh it and take his own. Rav Ḥisda dismissed him, and applied to him the verse "the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the righteous" (Proverbs 13:22).
bava_kamma-119a-7-7.why: It follows a dispute over whether an informer's property may be destroyed, where one view cites a verse that what the wicked prepare the just will wear; Rav Ḥisda cites a similar verse about a sinner's wealth passing to the righteous.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Owner of the field, who dismissed his sharecropper.

terms.meaning: A tenant who farms someone else's field in return for a share of the crop.

bava_kamma-119a-20-20.note: When Ravina came to Bei Meḥoza, the women of the town tossed chains and bracelets before him as charity, and he accepted them. Rabba Tosfa'a objected that charity collectors may accept only small gifts from women, not large ones. Ravina answered that for the people of Meḥoza, these were small things.
bava_kamma-119a-20-20.why: The discussion has just quoted the teaching that charity collectors may take only small gifts from women, since they may lack permission to give away costly things; this story tests how that rule applies.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who collected charity in Bei Meḥoza.

people.name: Rabba Tosfa’a
people.about: Challenged Ravina for accepting jewelry from women.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early rabbinic period that was not included in the Mishna.

bava_kamma-112b-1-1.note: Rabbi Yirmeya's dispute with his young brother-in-law over his late father-in-law's house reached Rabbi Abbahu. He asked whether they had not heard what Rav Yosef bar Hama said in Rabbi Oshaya's name: when a child takes his slaves into someone else's field and says "It is mine," the court does not wait until he grows up. It removes the field from him at once, and when he is grown he may bring witnesses and his claim will be examined.
bava_kamma-112b-1-1.why: Rabbi Avin had refused to hear witnesses against a minor; Rabbi Abbahu's ruling would let Rabbi Yirmeya win. The Gemara rejects the comparison: the boy holds the house from his father, unlike the child in Rabbi Oshaya's case.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: The Sage the dispute finally reaches, who cites Rabbi Oshaya's ruling.

people.name: Rav Yosef bar Hama
people.about: Reports Rabbi Oshaya's ruling about a child who seizes a field.

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya
people.about: The Sage whose ruling about a child claiming a field Rabbi Abbahu cites.

terms.meaning: Present people who saw the relevant events to testify in court; here, the child may prove his claim once he is an adult.
